abstract: Abstract Global mean sea level (GMSL) rise has accelerated over the last three decades, with satellite altimetry indicating an acceleration of 0.07 ± 0.03 mm/yr 2 over 1993–2023. However, the specific contributions of Greenland and Antarctica to this acceleration budget have remained insufficiently quantified. We extend satellite gravimetry estimates of Greenland and Antarctica ice mass changes back to 1993, enabling a comprehensive 31‐year assessment of their contributions to GMSL acceleration and providing an independent record for cross‐validation with other observational and modeling data sets. Ice mass loss has accelerated by −8.5 ± 4.0 Gt/yr 2 for Greenland and −4.6 ± 1.3 Gt/yr 2 for Antarctica from 1993 to 2023. These results are consistent across multiple data sets and collectively account for 51% of the observed GMSL acceleration. Mountain glaciers contribute an additional 0.01 mm/yr 2 to GMSL acceleration, bringing the total land ice contribution to 0.05 ± 0.01 mm/yr 2 and thereby partially closing the budget.

readout.label: Share of GMSL acceleration from ice sheets

summary: Ice loss from Greenland and Antarctica has sped up, and together they explain about half of the faster sea level rise seen by satellites. The team extended satellite gravity-based ice mass records back to 1993 and checked them against other data sets. Even with mountain glaciers added, the land ice budget only partly closes the observed acceleration.
title: Greenland and Antarctica Dominate Recent Acceleration in Global Mean Sea Level Rise: 1993–2023
